title: How to Use Average Daily Range (ADR) with PDH / PDL — No More Fakeouts
description: Learn how to use ADR with PDH and PDL, open targets, wick size, and daily range to identify valid continuation setups.

body.text: Introduction
Previous day high and previous day low are some of the easiest draws on liquidity to trade.
But taking out PDH or PDL does not automatically mean continuation.
The question is simple: how much ADR is left when price takes the level?
If price takes PDH or PDL early in the daily range, continuation can still be valid.
If price takes the level after most of the range has already been exhausted, do not expect the same expansion.
ADR gives you a mechanical way to measure that.
What Is ADR?
ADR stands for average daily range.
It measures the average range of a daily candle.
For example, if three daily candles have ranges of 297 points, 379 points, and 314 points, the total range is 990 points.
Divide 990 by three days and the ADR is 330 points.
Total daily range ÷ number of days = ADR
Ideally, use more days when calculating ADR. The example simply shows how the calculation works.
Start With The Range
Once you have your ADR, look at how much of the current daily range price has already used.
Then look at PDH or PDL.
If price takes PDH after only using a small portion of the ADR, there is still room for expansion.
If price takes PDL after only using a small portion of the ADR, the same logic applies.
The process is straightforward. Check the ADR, measure the range already used, identify PDH or PDL, and then look for open targets in the direction of the move.
When Continuation Makes Sense
Imagine the ADR is 900 points.
Price takes PDH after moving only 300 points.
There is still plenty of range left.
If there is also an open target above, continuation has room to develop.
The same applies below PDL.
If price takes PDL after using only a small portion of the ADR and there is an open target below, continuation can still make sense.
You are not expecting continuation because PDH or PDL was taken.
You are expecting it because there is still range available and a target left to reach.
When The Range Is Already Used
Now take the opposite example.
The ADR is 900 points and price has already moved 700 points before taking PDH.
There is not much range left.
Price could still continue another 200 points, but that does not mean you should expect it.
Most of the daily range has already been used.
At that point, consolidation, retracement, or reversal becomes more reasonable.
The same applies when price takes PDL after already using most of the ADR.
The level being taken does not change the amount of range price has left.
Wick Size Matters
A large opposing move can change the entire expectation.
Price may start the day with a small wick and plenty of room to reach a target.
Instead, price spends a long time forming a large opposing move.
That wick uses both time and range.
By the time price reaches PDH or PDL, much of the ADR may already be gone.
Now the same level has a different context.
Price can still reach the level, but expecting another large expansion after it is less logical.
This is why ADR needs to be combined with wick size and the way the daily candle is forming.
Open Targets Matter
ADR tells you how much range is available.
You also need to know what price can reach within that range.
If price takes PDH, has plenty of ADR left, and there is an open target above, that target can become the draw.
If price takes PDL with range left and an open target below, the same logic applies.
But if price has already taken the target, the expectation changes.
There may still be ADR left, but there is no longer the same open target supporting continuation.
Price can still expand.
It can also consolidate, retrace, or reverse.
Know When To Wait
Sometimes the best decision is to wait for a new daily candle.
If price has already used most of the ADR and then takes PDH or PDL, there may not be enough range left for another meaningful expansion.
Rather than forcing continuation late in the daily candle, wait for the new daily open.
Now you have a new daily range to work with.
This is especially important after a large opposing move that has already consumed a significant amount of time and range.
The Mechanical Rule
The rule is simple.
If price takes PDH or PDL and there is plenty of ADR left, continuation can be valid.
If price takes the level after most of the ADR has already been used, do not expect the same expansion.
Then look at the open target and the daily structure.
If the target is still open and there is enough range left to reach it, continuation has room to develop.
If the target has already been taken or the daily range is close to exhaustion, adjust your expectation.
Final Thoughts
Taking PDH or PDL does not automatically mean continuation.
Look at the range price has already used.
Look at the range that remains.
Look at the open targets.
Look at how the daily candle formed.
When the range and target support continuation, the move can continue.
When the range is exhausted, do not force it.
Wait for a new daily candle and reassess.
